sections.html:
The Johnson County seat lies about 20 miles south of Indianapolis and 90 miles north of Louisville, Kentucky, at the crossing of Interstate 65 and U.S. 31. Population is estimated at 26,743. That makes Franklin a small city next to a very large one, with many residents commuting north.

Growth was fastest from 1990 to 2000, adding more than 6,500 people. Plat records start in 1823, and cityhood came in 1861. Its housing therefore ranges from the Franklin Commercial Historic District and the Martin Place Historic District to subdivisions built during the growth years.

Heavy water in June 2008 pushed Canary Creek, Hurricane Creek and related waterways out of their banks. More than 100 houses were damaged or destroyed, and some whole neighborhoods were hit. The city and county then bought out flooded properties, using about $8.5 million in federal money to remove 107 homes. One neighborhood of about 70 small homes was cleared and has since been reforested by volunteers, who planned 4,000 to 4,500 trees. The parks department maintains the site.

Flood maps have been a sore point. Many proposed FEMA changes involved Canary Ditch, which runs through the north and west sides of the city, and about 70 percent of Franklin's industrial areas fell in the 100-year flood zone under one proposal. An insurance agent estimated that homeowners in newly designated areas could need coverage costing $1,500 or more a year.

  • Check where your parcel falls on FEMA's current flood map before listing.
  • Find out from your insurer if a flood policy exists on the house, and its cost.
  • Pull together repair records and permits if the house flooded in 2008 or later.

Where houses were bought out, open ground remains. A street beside the old flood area may now face trees and trails rather than neighbors. Demolition of flood-damaged homes began in 2010, and donations from residents plus grants from the Johnson County Community Foundation paid for the trees, trail markers and paths.

Own a house near a former buyout site? Share its history with buyers along with any elevation or insurance papers. People take bad news better when it comes from the seller.

Nearly all of the city is in Franklin Community Schools, home of Franklin Community High School, with five in-person elementary schools and a virtual school for grades 5 to 12. A sliver in the north is covered by Clark-Pleasant Community School Corporation, so look up the address before telling a buyer which schools apply.

Freight rail runs through town on the Louisville and Indiana Railroad. Pilots can use Franklin Flying Field, about 3.5 miles south of downtown, and Indianapolis International Airport lies about 28 miles northwest. Bus service comes from Access Johnson County. Manufacturers with plants in town include Toyota, NSK, KYB and Mitsubishi.

When a Johnson County house sells for money, seller and buyer sign a Sales Disclosure Form. The assessor looks it over, then it is filed with the county auditor, who cannot take the deed without it (Indiana Code 6-1.1-5.5). The fee is $20. Foreclosure, divorce, probate and condemnation transfers are exempt. The closing company usually fills it in.

The Johnson County Treasurer collects property tax at 86 W. Court Street, in the West Annex Building downtown. Call 317-346-4330. The spring half is due May 10 and the fall half November 10. Pay within 30 days after a due date and the penalty is 5 percent. After that it is 10 percent. The state calendar nudges a date by a day when it falls on a weekend.

  • Ways to pay: online, phone, mail, in person, the drop box outside the West Annex Building, or a handful of local banks.
  • Cards cost extra. Electronic and mailed checks do not.
  • Request a payoff number before you pick a closing date.

Five banks take payments if you bring the original coupon: First Financial Bank, First Merchants Bank, First National Bank, Horizon Bank and Mutual Savings Bank. An online card payment adds 2.5 percent with a $1.50 minimum, and Visa debit adds $3.95 per transaction. Those fees can change, so look at the treasurer's site first.

sections.h2: Selling a flood-affected or older Franklin house
sections.html:
How a Franklin buyer sees a house depends partly on its water history. Damage from 2008, a wet basement or a lot near Canary Ditch all raise questions, and any lender will want the flood zone in writing. Gather your paperwork first and the surprises are fewer.

  • Repair receipts and permits for any flood work.
  • Insurance papers, including any flood policy and what it costs.
  • Elevation information, if you have it.
  • Notes about what you know of any nearby buyout site.

Selling as-is does not excuse you from being honest about the house. What it changes is who pays for the condition: the buyer prices it in, so nobody asks you to fix things, and no appraisal can derail the sale.

Begin by sending the address and a few notes. After we tour the house, a written offer follows. Accept it and a title company runs the title search, drafts the deed and the Sales Disclosure Form, and books the closing for the day you choose. Proceeds first retire any mortgage or tax balance.

Get the tax figure from the treasurer early. An estate sale needs the court paperwork and heirs' names on the first call, and a tenant's lease belongs in the pile too. If the sale is by an estate, the personal representative signs.

sections.h2: Why owners here sell for cash
sections.html: Franklin sits close enough to Indianapolis that buyers from both markets look at its homes, yet a house with flood history or years of deferred work can still sit unsold. Owners who inherited a property, landlords tired of a tenant, and families who need to move before a listing could finish are the usual cash sellers. The timeline is theirs to set, and a short one is possible when the title work is clean.

sections.h2: Ways to sell a house in Franklin
sections.html:
You can hire an agent, sell it yourself, or take a cash offer. Which one fits depends on the house and on how soon you need to be done.

  • A listing suits a house in good repair when you can wait for showings and a buyer's loan.
  • Selling yourself works if disclosures and negotiating do not scare you.
  • A cash offer is the better match for flood history, deferred repairs, a tenant or an estate still being settled.

We buy Franklin houses in whatever condition they are in. Request an offer, compare it with the other routes, and say no if it does not fit.

faqs.q: What county is Franklin, Indiana in?
faqs.a: Johnson County, where it is the seat. Indianapolis is about 20 miles north.

faqs.q: Was Franklin hit by a flood?
faqs.a: Yes, in June 2008, when creeks overflowed and more than 100 houses took damage or were lost. The city and county later bought out many of those homes.

faqs.q: Do I need flood insurance to sell a house in Franklin?
faqs.a: Selling does not require it. A buyer's lender might, if the home lies in a mapped flood zone, so look at the current FEMA map for your parcel.

faqs.q: When are Johnson County property taxes due?
faqs.a: The spring half is due May 10 and the fall half November 10. Late within 30 days costs 5 percent, and later costs 10 percent.
